subtopic: MESSAGE FROM THE SENATE WITH RESPECT TO SENATE AMENDMENTS TO BILL NO. 21

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MESSAGE FROM THE SENATE WITH RESPECT TO SENATE AMENDMENTS TO BILL NO. 21
speechtext:
I desire to say a word of explanation with respect to order No. 6 under government orders with regard to Bill No. 21, to provide for limiting the hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight in the day and forty-eight in the week, in accordance with the convention concerning the application of the principle of the eight hour day or of the forty-eight hour week adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization of the League of Nations, in accordance with the labour part of the treaty of Versailles of the 28th June, 1919. In the certificate that went to the Senate accompanying the message, it is indicated that the Commons had agreed to all the Senate amendments except as regards the consequential amendment which I moved, to amendment No. 9. In the motion that is recorded in our house it appeared that we agreed to eight amendments, did not agree to amendments Nos. 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14. and moved our consequential amendment with respect to number 9. The Senate, taking the fact from the message and not from the certificate, sent back to this house the bill to have amendments Nos. 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 dealt with by the house. I went over those amendments fully at the time they were before the house and said that we concurred in them as they were not matters of importance, but in order that the matter may now be regularized owing to the' conflict between the certificate and the motion as recorded, I move:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours that this house agrees to the amendments Nos. 10, 11. 12, 13 and 14 made by the Senate to the Bill No. 21, an act to provide for limiting the hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight in the day and forty-eight in the week, in accordance with the convention concerning the application of the principle of the eight hour day or of the forty-eight hour week adopted by the general conference of the international labour organ-

Dominion Day Adjournment
ization of the League of Nations, in accordance with the labour part of the treaty of Versailles of the 28th June, 1919, without any amendment.
And_ that the clerk of the house do carry the said message to the Senate.
We have not dealt, nor does this propose to deal with the consequential amendment which I moved the other day in regard to Senate amendment No. 9, and with which the Senate has indicated it does not agree. That means a conference or further action between the two houses. I am leaving that for the moment and will endeavour to dispose of it at the next sitting when I am further informed in connection with it. But in order that there may be conformity between the motion and the certificate, I am moving the motion aforesaid.

speechtext:
If the house will direct its attention to Bill No. 99, and to the votes and proceedings of this house indicating the action of the Senate I think they will agree that we cannot possibly accept the so-called amendment of that chamber. It will be recalled that Bill No. 99 of this house provided for the extension of the provision of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act of 1932, chapter 35, statutes of 1932-33 as amended by chapter 24 of the statutes of the present session, until March 31, 1936. There was an extension until June 30, 1935, but the Senate when it received the bill proceeded to provide that the whole radio set up, the measure known as the radio statute^ should only last until next March. Of course that is not an 92582-258
amendment, that is a declaration- of policy entirely at variance with that which the government has declared time and again to this house. I therefore move, seconded- by Mr. Guthrie:
That the house inform their honours that we are unable to agree to their amendments, inasmuch as they have made a declaration of policy not consistent with the avowed policy of the government, and that they insist upon the bill as it left this house being enacted.

It is moved by Mr. Bennett, seconded by Mr. Guthrie.
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours that this house disagrees with their amendments to Bill No. 99, an act respecting radio broadcasting, for the reasons set forth by the Prime Minister, and that the clerk of the House carry the said message to the Senate.
Motion agreed to.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by -the Senate to Bill No. 62, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act.
He said: The Senate made a slight amendment to this measure, providing that instead of it coming into force on the day on which it was assented to, as it would, it should come into force on the first of July. If the house agrees to that proposal, as I ask it now to do, we will endeavour to have -the act assented to this afternoon so that it will begin on the first day of the month-, thereby making it, simpler from the standpoint of superannuation- and keeping the books of the country.
Motion- agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I gather from
what the right bon. Prime Minister has just said that the government intends to drop the controversial measure, the elections bill, because he refers to only one other measure, that not being controversial. If that is the case it will materially shorten the session and insure speedier prorogation. Also, if the committee dealing with the grain- bill- has still to confer and reach a conclusion -with regard to its provisions possibly the time of all hon. members would be spent more profitably if that committee continued its work and the rest of us looked- on over th-e period of July first. Once that bill is settled I believe I can say on behalf of the opposition that provided the bill I -referred to w-ith respect to thie elections act is withdrawn, the rest of the order paper will not take many hours to conclude.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Of course the bill to amend the elections act will have- to be given second reading, because there are sections in it, such as that in regard to the hours during which advance polls are kept open, and the waiver of preparation of fresh lists for byelections, matters of that sort, which must be dealt with, but those are not controversial. I can say frankly that it is not intended to proceed with the controversial sections, in v-iew of the strong expressions of opinion that came from the other side yesterday with respect to them, although I think possibly most hon. members may have received a small pamphlet from Great Britain in which the whole fate of democracy is regarded as being at stake because th-e will of minorities represents the life of -governments, and pointing out how undesirable that is. But that is a matter with which the minister himself will deal when- he moves second reading of the bill.

If it is acceptable to the house I would confer further with members of the committee, and later without notice, if it is possible, move that when the house adjourns it adjourn until Tuesday afternoon at 3 o'clock. If that meets with the approval- of the house I shall be glad to give some further information about it at that time.

In regard to
the elections bill m-ay I say that as far as the part referring to the transferable vote is concerned, the attitude of hon. members on this -side is and has -been that this is not the time to introduce -as farre-aching a departure from our electoral methods as a transferable vote would be. As I stated at the outset it is th-e sectional character of the measure introduced to which we take strong exception. The- question of th-e principle involved in the transferable vote is another matter, one that I think could be taken up to much better effect at the beginning of a new parliament, rather than when the days of an old parliament have expired.
The Prime Minister, I think, will find that hon. members on this side will be in agreement with hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to Monday next, provided we can make the arrangement indicated.

Civil Aviation-
Expenses in connection with the control of civil aviation, airways, government and public airports and grants to aeroplane clubs.- further amount required, $497,900.

Mr. Chairman, this vote increases by over $200,000 the vote in the main estimates. At that time we voted the sum of $250,000 and we are now asked to vote this much larger sum of $497,900. I wonder if the minister would explain the increase and give a brief resume of what has been done by the government in connection with the promotion of civil aviation.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, due to
the increased use of aeroplanes there is of necessity additional work in the department. Inspection services and investigations consequent upon accidents which have occurred fall to the inspectors of the department. In consequence it is necessary all the time to keep abreast of the work, which has been increasing with considerable rapidity. Then, work is being undertaken to keep abreast of the times with regard to direction beacons. It is hoped very shortly to have radio control of that section between Ottawa and Montreal, for instance, and gradually it is expected that radio direction beams will be erected across Canada,-although that is a long way ahead. Provision is made in the vote for acquiring land at ten different points scattered across the dominion for the purpose of proceeding with the project of having emergency fields across Canada. In the majority of cases crown lands either in the right of the dominion or in the right of the provinces have been available, and by arrangement they have been set aside for these emergency fields. Hitherto with the exception of cleaning, clearing, level-
Supply-Aviation

ling, a certain amount of drainage and the building of certain roads and fences little has been done. In various parts of Canada relief camp workers have been used for that purpose. There are ten places, four being in the province of British Columbia, three in Quebec, one in Nova Scotia, one in New Brunswick and one in Ontario, where it is thought desirable to begin work on what eventually will be emergency fields in a chain right across Canada.
Then, in connection with stores and equipment there is a sum for the purchase and installation of the lighting equipment on the two sites to which I have referred, and provision for the purchase of high frequency transmitters and receivers, and other pieces of machinery of that description, to get on with the transmitting of the beams.

Quebec?

The agreement arrived
at between the department and the aeroplane clubs has been reviewed, and the aeroplanes granted to the existing clubs were granted at the same time. They have had little done to the planes, and they are almost on their last legs.

statement which has been prepared in this connection. I had it in my other book of estimates, but it is not before me now.

Lemieux island; a

done under this appropriation be done by relief labour?

ditional construction under the provisions of the Public Works Act and getting it back where it has been contended all the time it should be.

Item agreed to.
River St. Lawrence ship channel dredges- (b) to provide for the maintenance and operation of the government ship channel fleet and government shipyard'-further amount required, $250,000.

Some weeks ago
I asked for certain information which would have enabled me to have a better understanding of this item but although this question was allowed to stand as an order for return, the return has not yet been tabled. I should like to know how many dredges were owned by the department in 1928.

I am sorry but I
have not that information.

How many were
owned in 1935?
Offhand I should say about ten or twelve.

When were they
acquired?

Some years ago;
some were built by the department in the shipyard at Sorel.

What did they
cost?

That is the trouble. My hon. friend has been complaining of delays in supplying information he has requested from my department. These details are complicated and my officials have not had enough time to pick up all the information. As I told my hon. friend the other day, they are working at it, and as soon as possible it will be laid on the table of the house.

That is not sufficient. Surely if the minister's department is properly organized, he knows how many dredges there are at the present time and what those dredges cost. No minister can tell me that such information is not readily available within the department. It is now three weeks since the information was asked for.

For the information of my hon. friend as to this item, we are asking for a further amount of 8250,000 in order to complete as soon as possible with our own dredges the cleaning up of the ship channel from the sea to Montreal to a depth

Supply-Marine-Miscellaneous
of thirty-five feet at the level of 1897 or thirty-two and a half feet at the level of October, 1934. That is the only purpose. The work has become more and more pressing on account of the increase in the tonnage of ships coming to Montreal, and as we are anxious, as all Canadians should be, that this channel be completed during this present season of navigation, that is why we are asking for this further amount.

The purpose of submitting these estimates to the house is that the house may be apprised of the necessity of the works proposed to be undertaken. This is a large item amounting to $250,000, and I should like to know a little more about it. The very fact that the minister finds it so hard to give me the information makes me a little bit more curious. How many scows are there at the present time attending these dredges?

I have not the information at the present time, and I do not think it has anything to do with the vote in question. As a matter of fact this item is not for the purpose of building or purchasing dredges or scows; it is for the purpose of putting into commission dredges and scows owned by my department and which for reasons of economy have been laid up during these last years.
That is the very point. I would like to know how many there are altogether in the fleet.
In the last two years we have had on the St. Lawrence, only four dredges, two working below Quebec and two above.
How many altogether?
I have already told my hon. friend that I think we have ten or twelve dredges belonging to the department.
What percentage of the dredging in the St. Lawrence river from Montreal to Quebec has been given to private contractors?

I have not that information before me, I am sorry. All I know is that we are carrying out the program which was laid down by our predecessors before 1930, and the work on the portion of the St. Lawrence which was left to be completed by the dredges of the department is a little bit 925S2-259
in arrears. That is why I want this further amount to supplement the $1,140,000 voted in the main estimates for our own fleet, in order to complete the cleaning up of the channel between the sea and Montreal.
The minister has a fleet, but he cannot tell how many ships there are in it or what they cost. Is it to be the policy from now on to do all the dredging by the fleet owned by the department?

It is not our policy,
because the department does not have power-full enough dredges to do certain works in the St. Lawrence. Our dredges are not all up to date and we have not powerful enough dredges for that purpose. As regards certain works where there is rock for instance, we have tried to do the job with out own dredges, but it was so costly to the department, five or six times more than it would cost under contract, that we had to abandon it. It is the scheme adopted by our predecessors that we are proceeding with.

What is the cost
to the department of supervising the work done by those contractors to whom the minister has just referred?

As I have told the
committee, I have not the information at hand. I know the department has many engineers surveying the St. Lawrence during the whole navigation season. We have also on contractors' dredges, following the operations and making reports to the department, two or three inspectors, depending on the circumstances. If the dredge is working twenty-four hours a day, we have three inspectors; if it works only during the daytime, we have only two. But as to the amount expended for that purpose, I have not the information before me. I can say to my hon. friend that the supervision is complete and very satisfactory to the departs meat.
Have any government dredges been sold to or used by private contractors?

Not since I have
been in charge, to my knowledge. I may add this, that since my department has acquired from the Department of Railways and Canals the dredge Churchill, this dredge was put at the disposal of the Saint John dry dock for the demolition of berths one, two, three and four which were burned three or four years ago as my hon. friend will remember. That is the only circumstance



Supply-Marine-Miscellaneous
where a dredge was put under rent or loan to a contractor. When I say "loan," I might explain:	The St. John dry dock company
had undertaken the demolition at cost plus four per cent or five per cent and that dredge was put at their disposal.

Have any dredges
or scows been sold1 to the Quebec harbour commission?	[DOT]
Not to my knowledge; I do not think so. The Quebec harbour commission might have sold an old dredge, but I do not think the commission has bought any dredge.

Have any floating
scows or rook breakers or stone lifters been supplied to the contractors?

As I told my hon.
friend a minute ago, I have not the information.

It is rather curious that we are being asked to vote a further amount of $250,000 to provide for the maintenance and operation of the government ship channel fleet and government shipyard, and the minister, after having been asked for this information for some weeks, has apparently not been able so far to ascertain facts that ought to be ascertainable within a few hours in any well organized1 department. I cannot understand the minister taking that attitude. If he wants this $250,000, the least he can do, like other ministers, is to have the information at hand, and I think we are entitled to ask that this item stand until we receive the information. At present we cannot vote intelligently on this item.

I do not tihink the
fact of lending a scow or other equipment to a private firm or otherwise has anything to do with this item which is to supplement item (b) in vote 139 which concerns our own fleet. It is not for the purpose of purchasing any equipment, dredges, scows, tugs or anything, it is only to put into commission the tugs, scows and dredges we already have belonging to the department, and to pay men to be put on those dredges.

Then on that basis the minister can surely tell me how many dredges they have. If he wants $250,000 more to put them into commission can he not tell me how many we have? Several weeks ago I asked how many we had in 1928, how many in 1929, in 1930, in 1931, in 1932, 1933, 1934 and 1935, and apparently he cannot tell me.

If the information mentioned by my hon. friend were the only thing asked in his long list of questions he would have had the answer long ago. But there are some details asked which involve a great deal of work by my engineers, and at present the larger number of my engineers are on the St. Lawrence or elsewhere.

This is not a question that, pertains to engineering, and the minister knows that well. The information is in the department, it is a matter of bookkeeping, and the minister could get it within three hours if he wanted to give it. I think we ought to have it before proceeding with this item. A quarter of a million dollars is asked to put certain dredges into commission, and the minister refuses to inform us how many they have and their history.

I told my hon. friend that we have about ten or twelve. But it does not matter much if we have twenty or twenty-five so far as this item is concerned, because we have only four in commission at the present time, and with this amount I might put one or perhaps two more into cammission. That would make five or six out of ten.
I am asking what percentage of work is to be done by these dredges of the department and what percentage is to be done by private contractors.

Offhand I would say the works were divided almost equally in the scheme of my hon. friend which we are proceeding with. But the department, owing to our equipment not being up to date, and the fact that we have not large funds available, is behind with its work. I would like to have this further amount in order to complete the cleaning up of the channel this season. This work is asked for by the province of Quebec and I think should be approved by all citizens of Canada. It is very important for Canada that large ocean shipping should be brought to the heart of Canada. That is why we want to keep our channel in proper shape.
Can the minister tell me how many firms tendered, for this work?

From memory I cannot say. I know tenders were asked when that contract was let in May, 1930, by 'the previous administration. My hon. friend knows that the firms equipped to do that sort of work on the St. Lawrence are few.

Supply-Marine-Miscellaneous

How many are
there?
There might be two or three firms in Canada.
Is there more than one firm doing the work?

Yes, I can tell my hon. friend that there was a main contract and also subcontracts to two other firms, I think. But there are certain works for the execution, of which I do not think more than two firms in Canada have equipment.
What are the names of those firms?

I think the General Dredging Company Limited had the main contract, and the other firms which had their share of it are, I think, the Canadian Dredging Company and J. P. Porter & Sons, Limited. They are very reliable firms, and the works are done to the great satisfaction of my engineers.
Is it proposed that when the dredges are reconditioned the department is to use them itself, or to let them out to one or other of these contractors?

The policy of this government has been to keep for our own department the equipment we had in 1930. Moreover we have purchased from the Department of Railways and Canals the Churchill, a powerful dredge. She is a,t Saint John at the present time, working at the reconditioning of berths 1, 2, 3 and 4. We do not intend to sell our equipment.
I am not speaking of selling, but does the department itself operate its own dredges and scows, or does it on occasion give the use of them under certain conditions to private contractors?
The dredges and scows which we do not use, on account of the small amounts voted by this house for the last three or four years, have been laid up and kept in a reasonable state of repair.

That is not my question. When this $250,000 is expended and our fleet is reconditioned is it the policy of the department to operate the whole of that fleet itself, or are certain partis of the equipment to be given over to be used by private contractors?
The policy of this government is to employ our whole fleet when we have a vote large enough for the purpose. We dlo not rent or lend our equipment to any private firm.
What is this $250,000 for? Is it for repairs to the existing fleet or to operate the fleet?

The greater part of this amount is to put into commission one or two dredges of the department' which are in a fairly good state of repair. It is to employ more men on our fleet. It may be that small repairs will be necessary, because the vote covers also expenses of the plant at Sorel. But the largest part of this amount is to put into commission one or two dredges.
We are pretty well along in the dredging season. Has the department decided whether it is one dredge or two in addition to what they have been operating for the last few years ?

I had asked for a larger amount than this, but obtained $250,000 from the treasury board. I am told by my officials that we might be able to put two more dredges into commission. It may be that we shall have to shorten the season when the amount is exhausted, but we intend to put on two more dredges.

I have some knowledge of dredging and I want to say that if you intended to do dredging this year the dredges should have been equipped and at work before this. I see that under item No. 139 of the main estimates $1,140,000 was voted for this same purpose, the same vote the minister had in 1934-35. Now he comes along with an additional $250,000 and he does not know whether one or two additional dredges will be required. The minister does not seem to know anything in particular about what is going to be done with this $250,000. I agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre; I think this item should stand until the minister knows something about the number of dredges it is intended to operate and what will be done with this amount of money.
I have given a fairly good explanation.
It may be satisfactory to the minister but it is an awfully poor explanation so far as the committee is concerned.

I am told by my officials that with two more dredges working in

Supply-Marine-Miscellaneous
the channel 'between Quebec and Montreal we may expect the thirty-five foot channel to be completed probably next September. It is our intention to put on these two additional dredges for as long as possible with this amount of money, in addition to the other four dredges that have been in commission since the beginning of the season. I think that explanation should be satisfactory.

If I am permitted to butt into this highly technical discussion I should like to ask the minister if it is not true that dredging is much cheaper when it is done by private firms than when it is done with the departmental apparatus, and if that is so I should like to know why.

I cannot admit the proposition put forward by my hon. friend. It may be so; it all depends on the equipment and the material. Of course a powerful, up-to-date dredge would do more work than another dredge not so powerful. The trouble is that the department has not the powerful dredges needed in certain parts of the St. Lawrence. It may be also that the dredging done by a private firm .may 'be less costly because of the wages paid. The department is supposed to pay better wages than private firms. I do not affirm that fact, but I think that is the case.

I understand that what the hon. gentleman has said is just a preface to his answer, and I am waiting for this answer. I asked if there was any reason why it should be cheaper to have dredging done by private firms than by the department. That is my question; it is right to the point, and I should like to have a straight answer.

I want to be frank with my hon. friend; I think dredging done by private firms costs less to the department than the dredging done by the department, but the department must maintain its dredging because we have a great deal of cleaning up to do in the channel, and we need the fleet for that purpose.
I thank the minister. I am satisfied with his answer.

I suppose the minister has some information as to the yardage that has to come out of the St. Lawrence that must be handled by these large dredges; I presume the engineers of the department have taken soundings in the channel. Can the minister say what yardage must be handled by the large dredges and the approximate yardage that can be handled by the departmental dredges?

I think I have the information at the department; I am sorry I do not have it here. I can tell my hon. friend that the dredging in the St. Lawrence, under the 1930 contract, has been going on steadily and is now pretty well advanced.

Was not the water in the
St. Lawrence very low this year?
Yes, at one time, but in the last three weeks the water has come up over a foot and a half, and at the present time the level is very satisfactory.

Would the minister
tell the committee whether the contract entered into in 1930, which is being continued, calls for the completion of the work which the department dredges cannot handle?
Yes.

Is the contract on the
same price basis as when it was entered into in 1930?

No, the price has
been lowered by two or three dollars a cubic yard. It has been lowered by at least two dollars for the further hard work.

Was this contract of
1930 let to one company?
Yes, and part of the contract was transferred to the other firms I have already mentioned.

What company got the
original contract?
The General Dredging Company, Limited.

And they sublet some
of that contract to other companies?

I think they have
transferred part of their contract.

Just what proportion
of the contract has been transferred and what are the companies that secured the subcontracts from the original company?
I could not give the exact figures but I think the two other companies secured nearly one-half the whole job.
Of the original contract?
The original contract.

Can the minister give
the committee any information as to the price at which these sub-contracts were let?

Supply-Interior

I am under the impression that it was a transfer of contract. It may be that the company that secured the original contract, being responsible for the work, might have retained five or ten per cent of the amount, but it was practically a transfer of contract.

But in view of the fact that the department let this one continuous contract for all this work surely when subcontracts are made the department must have information not only as to the companies to which the sub-contracts were let but also as to the prices at which they were let, because the minister has stated that the original company must be responsible for the proper completion of the work.

When we came into
power in 1930 these sub-contracts had been let and the companies were at work. I have not the contracts or sub-contracts here; I would not like to mislead this committee, but I think it was practically a transfer of part of the contract.

If it was a transfer of
part of the contract-and we will accept that explanation-then the minister's department must have been a party to that part of the transfer. Therefore he must have information in his office as to the terms upon which the transfer was made. That is the information I should like to have.

If the hon. member
desires to have the information I should be glad to supply it; no doubt I can supply it, but I have not the information with me.

Could the minister
have it to-night at eight o'clock?

I could write the
hon. member and tell him the facts.
Could you get it tonight?

I do not know; it
is five-thirty, and the office will be closed. I could write, however.

I should like to have
this information before the committee because in my judgment it is very important to have a little more information about dredging contracts in the St. Lawrence. If the minister could see his way clear to let it stand until such time as he could get the information, I would appreciate it very much.

The minister left the
impression that the wages paid by private
contractors were not as high as those which might be paid by the government. I should like to know whether the fspr wages clause is made a part of private contracts.
The fair wages clause is inserted.

Why is it that they were
paying lower wages than the government were paying?
I thought they were.

The minister is not
sure.

For instance, the
captain on a dredge of a private concern might receive a little less salary than a captain on a government dredge; I am not quite sure about it. The wages paid to labourers are the same, because they are under a fair wages scale.

In view of the statement made by the minister to the effect that government dredges could not compete with privately owned dredges because of the fact that they were paying a lower wage scale, I believe we should have further information concerning the vote before we are asked to pass it. Perhaps the minister would accede to the reasonable request that the item stand until the information is received.

I have no objection.
Item stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be pleased to undertake the forwarding to the minister of the hon. member's remarks.
What are the details of this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the absence of the minister I have not the information, but if the hon. member desires I shall see that he receives it.

There is something here in regard to the dominion fuel board. Now, there has been some high pressure canvassing since the beginning of this session, and there has been lobbying in the interests of peat. Peat, it is said, is going to save this country if a subsidy is granted to a peat firm. This is most ridiculous, and we should not be bothered by any canvassing on the part of lobbyists in the House of Commons, asking for a grant for peat. Every member has been imposed upon since the beginning of the session by invitations to entertainments and otherwise, for the purpose of lending encouragement to the new industry. We have had enough of that, and I hope the government will be sensible enough not to give any consideration to such interested propaganda.

Supply-Labour-Annuities
We do not know anything about it. The gentleman says he represents some Scotch company, but nobody knows whether it is Scotch or Danish or Nordic. It is a real imposition for members to have these fellows running after them and, as I say, I hope the government will be sensible enough not to pay any attention to such a request.

I cannot allow the remarks of my hon. friend to pass unchallenged. I do not intend to refer to any company whatever, or to discuss lobbying or canvassing; but to say that we should not study the peat situation because something of this sort might have been done is absolutely contrary to common sense. Peat is a natural resource of this country; it is a fuel to be found in the central provinces and it might be utilized by the people to great advantage. It would probably result in curtailing importations of fuel, and it would give work to local men in the processing of it. I would recommend very strongly that further investigation be made into the possibilities of this natural resource. I think the government should carry on investigations in the interests of the Canadian people.

The committee is perhaps under the impression that my hon. friend from
Prescott disagrees with the remarks I have made. As a matter of fact, I fully agree with him, and what I said was not intended to discourage experiments on the part of the government in connection with peat. It is a natural resource and I think the government should continue those experiments and choose the best fields in order to secure the best sort of peat available. But that is a very different thing from saying that a subsidy should be granted to a private concern. My hon. friend from Prescott has not said anything that conflicts with the views I have expressed.

Annuities Act-further amount required, $65,000.

The sale of government annuities is, I understand, pretty well in the hands of certain officials throughout the country who have offices in the larger towns and cities and who do their work on the commission basis. I am informed that at the beginning of this year the commission was cut approximately forty per cent. Offhand, I would say that this is a very drastic reduction in the remuneration which is allowed these agents, and I am impelled to ask-I suppose it would be the Minister of Finance
under the circumstances-whether this reduction is made in the interests of economy or in order to discourage the sale of government annuities, and also whether similar reductions have been made in other phases of this particular branch. Either we have allowed too much in the past or we are not allowing enough now. What is the explanation of the reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Until my hon. friend said that there had been a reduction in the amount of the commission paid, I had not heard that there had been, so that I shall have to make inquiry of the officials of the department to ascertain whether it is a fact. I shall endeavour to have the information if at all possible before the committee rises. I cannot answer the question offhand, but I can say that there has been no diminution in the applications for annuities; on the contrary, there has been a very marked increase in the demand. If I mistake not, the occasion for this vote, although I have not the details before me, arises because of the additional expense incurred as a result of the very largely increased demand for annuities which has been apparent throughout the year. However, I will endeavour to have the exact information before the committee rises.

I am satisfied with the reply which the minister has given in the meantime. I wonder whether he would say anything as to the attitude of the government towards annuities? Are they really in favour of extending the sale of annuities or would they prefer to see it gradually die out? I had the impression years ago that the annuities business of the government was not a remunerative one, and one would hardly blame the government if they did not encourage the sale of annuities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been no change in the policy which has obtained hitherto, not only under this government but under the preceding one as well; we have pursued the same policy. The sale of annuities has increased year by year, and that in itself is evidence that there has been no intention of discouraging it. I have no hesitation in frankly saying to my hon. friend that I believe that a government another year would be well advised to review the rates paid for annuities, because they are below the actuarial requirements.
Is not that probably the reason the business is increasing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That might very well be a contributing factor. As a matter of fact I
Supply-Labour

believe 'that they fail to carry themselves to the extent of $450,000 per annum, apart from the overhead. The carrying charge involves that annual drain upon the treasury, and I think the price of annuities might properly be increased to the point where they would carry themselves, apart from administration.
It might also be one of the reasons why the commissions have been cut.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to inquire with regard to the question .of commission.
What is the total amount of annuities in force at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have none of the data here, but I will endeavour to get it before the committee rises.

International Labour Conference-further amount required, $5,000.

This is a rather small amount. The government had some forms of convention through this organization, and the mistake that was made was to contend that these forms were binding like contracts. It was a great mistake of the government, though I see some of my hon. friends opposite smiling-one of them particularly on the treasury benches. He knows that I am right and he knows that these so-called conventions are not binding upon Canada and were merely an attempt to justify the new era and the new social legislation which was passed in an effort to save Canada economically. It was a great mistake and everyone regrets it. We find a vote of $1,000 for the administration of hours of labour, weekly rest and minimum wage acts. In addition there are other large amounts being provided to grease the wheels of this new machine. It is regrettable that a complete study of this whole matter was not left to the minister whom I saw smiling a minute ago. I know that with his profound knowledge of the law he would have told the government that they were mistaken. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) had been asked to look into this matter I am sure that with his great experience as a lawyer he would have said that it was no good. If the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) had been asked to make a special survey of the whole thing I am sure he would have said that it was no good. If my friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) had been asked to report I am sure his report would have been against all this. If the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) had been asked to look into this legislation

I am sure he would have said: We cannot go on with this. As it was, this was made up by third rate clerks and imposed upon the government by someone whom we all know. They were told they must accept it as it was, whether good or bad, just because it looked nice. This legislation was not drafted as a means of doing good, it was simply made to look nice. And it is going to cost a lot to pay for it all. I do not believe this legislation will work out and my deep conviction is that as soon as it is brought before the courts it will be declared to be void. We will then be no better off than we were before while those who have been appointed as members of these boards will join the ranks of the unemployed. Perhaps that is the only satisfaction we will get from the legislation.

Item agreed to.
Administration of hours of labour, weekly rest and minimum wages acts, $100,000.

The government
seems now to be showing some concern about the constitutionality of its measures and in view of that attitude I should like to know if the minister does not think it might be wise to consider testing the validity of one, two or three of these acts before entering upon their administration on too vast a scale?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is nothing I can add to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has said on one or two different occasions when similar questions were put to him by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). I shall direct the Prime Minister's attention to this question in the event of his desiring to enlarge upon what he has said previously.

The trouble is that in the early part of the session the Prime Minister did not seem to care much about the matter of constitutionality but during the latter part he has seemed to be greatly concerned. We should like to know just where the government stands now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I possessed the necessary legal background I might attempt to answer the question myself, but not having that I prefer to leave it to the Prime Minister.

I can quite appreciate the fact that no member of the government feels himself able to give an answer.

This so-called social legislation was the main issue in the provincial campaign in New Brunswick which ended yesterday and I think the answer was loud enough.
Will the minister give us the particulars of this expenditure?

All the measures mentioned come to a certain extent under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. I should like to see the officials appointed under these acts work in close cooperation, so far as that is possible, with the officials of the provincial governments. It would be most unfortunate if we should have within any province two sets of officials attempting to enforce similar legislation but working in opposite directions. I am sorry the Minister of Labour is not in his place to-night; he might be able to give the committee some idea as to how it is intended to appoint the, officials contemplated by this vote and how they will go about their work. I do not know whether the minister who is now in charge of this item can give that information, but I should like to know if it is the intention of the Department of Labour to have these officials work as far as possible in conjunction with the officials of the provincial governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will appreciate that I am not familiar with the details of the operation of this department; I have not had an opportunity of conferring with my colleague, nor do I know just what has been the practice of the department. Rut I have no hesitation in, saying that I think it would be sound policy on the part of any government to work in the closest possible cooperation with provincial governments having officials dealing with matters in a similar field. I know that in the Department of Fisheries, while I happened to be head of that department, as well as in the Department of Finance, I have been at pains to endeavour to work in the closest cooperation with the officials of the provincial govern-

meats, and indeed with the provincial governments themselves, where our objects have been in common. I think I should be safe in saying that it will be the policy of the Department of Labour, where it can do so to the advantage of the common cause, to work in the closest possible cooperation, with the officials of the various provincial administrations.

The government will
accomplish marvels if they work in cooperation with the provinces in matters conberping which the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction. They will put their n-ose into the business of the provinces, and it will be a great mistake. They have nothing to do with this matter; it belongs to the provinces. The only thing ,to do is to urge the provinces to enact legislation such as this,, if .possible, by orderly compromise, and I for one do not believe much in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry to differ with my hon. friend from Temiscouata. I may say to him that in the province from which he comes, to which the fisheries have been transferred, we work in the closest possible cooperation with the provincial government. Indeed, our officials not only exchange views, information and knowledge; on occasions when we could be of mutual assistance the province and the dominion have pooled their resources for the purpose of serving the Department of Fisheries of that province to greater advantage. I think it is all to the good that there should be the closest possible cooperation 'between the province and the dominion covering the common field.

Yes, but this is entirely different. I do not contend that there should be war between the federal and provincial governments; that is not my point of view at all. I am telling the committee that when one body, whether the dominion or the province, has exclusive jurisdiction the two bodies cannot cooperate because one has full power and only one can have full power. That is the contention I humbly submit to the committee. It is altogether different from cooperation in matters which may be considered from various viewpoints. For instance, the fisheries belonged to the dominion for a long time; they were transferred to the province of Quebec. Well and good; there must be cooperation to a certain extent between the dominion and the province. On the other hand it is entirely different to say that the dominion will take charge of something exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and that is what I am saying.

Supply-Pensions and National Health

In reply to my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Pouliot), may I say that it would not have been a bad thing at all if the federal government had maintained one or two fair wage officers in the province of Quebec, paid by the federal authority. The federal government let quite a large number of contracts in the province of Quebec, according to the evidence given before the price spreads committee, and if some of the fair wage provisions of those contracts had been enforced by the federal government certainly it would have done no harm to the province of Quebec.

I have just a word to say in reply to the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), and it is this: The hon. member for Temiscouata looked into the matter of minimum wages in this house long before the labour members from the west began to deal with it, and he pointed out a way to redress some wrongs with regard to wages a long time before my hon. friend and the members of his group took up the matter in this house. He did so because he knew the conditions that existed in that province. Here is the point: When my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group want something they want it by any means, whether it is right or wrong and whether or not it is done in the right way. They want it; they are just like children who want jam. This is not the right way. When we want something we must get it in the legal way in order that what we ask for may be endorsed by the courts should the occasion arise. If this government has no jurisdiction at all, when it sends inspectors to the province of Quebec, the province of Nova Scotia, the province of Manitoba, or the province of New Brunswick-I do not suppose that will happen now-to look after provincial business, the province may object and tell the inspectors to go back to Ottawa, that they have no business in that province. That is why it is so important to have this matter submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada in order that we may have some lead from the court in the matter. I do not object at all to the views expressed by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, but this is altogether different. My hon. friend from North Winnipeg must remember that whatever we may put in any federal enactment with regard to minimum wages in practice is only applicable to the extent that it is sanctioned by the courts which have to interpret the laws of this country according to the constitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. Much of the machinery in the mint is twenty years old. The major item is for what is known as Cottrell equipment. As a matter of fact there has been an escape of gases from the melting furnaces carrying precious metal to an extent of not less than 1,000 ounces of gold per year. We are putting in an apparatus which will wash the gases from the melting furnaces and it is guaranteed that we will recover not less than 1,000 ounces of gold per year. The net result will be that the whole expenditure will be covered in a little over three years' time.

The minister has had a request for help from the silver association of British Columbia. I wonder if he has considered granting them some assistance. I have a second question. How many silver dollars have been issued to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have had several communications from the silver association of British Columbia, and we feel that we have made a start in our assistance to those who have special regard for silver. There have been issued up to the moment $284,000 worth of silver dollars. It has not begun to meet the demand, but there is a limiting factor. We have only one machine in the mint capable of being adapted to the striking of the dollar coin, and at the same time there has been a tremendously heavy demand for the five cent and one cent coins, arising largely from the fact that sales taxes and amusement taxes have been imposed in various provinces and the demand for small change has been enormous. Since there is no substitute in coinage or notes for these smaller coins we have had to give the preference to them as against the silver dollar, which is comparatively a luxury coin that can have a substitute in the form of a note. But as rapidly as the limiting factor to which I have referred
is obviated we shall endeavour to meet the demand. I visited the mint this morning and they were striking dollar coins at the rate of sixty a minute.

Now they should be commended for the investigation being made by the tariff board, but it is too late; parliament will soon be prorogued, and all the legislation from 1930 to 1933 was passed without proper information because the government changed the situation with regard to the tariff board. And now, after the failure of their experiments, they see that the Liberal policy was right and they are trying to go back to it. But it is too late.

I am afraid
there will be considerable confusion in the accounts of this body. At one stage it will be known as the tariff board and at another stage it will be known as the dominion trade and industry commission. How are these two bodies to be distinguished? The trade and industry commission is under the tariff board, the chairman of the tariff board being also chairman of the commission. It seems to me there ought to be some distinction between the accounts of these two bodies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not had an opportunity to discuss the matter with the chairman of the tariff board, because before he went away I was ill, and he has been away for some little time in connection with the automobile and gasoline investigations. It is purely a question of accounting as to whether it relates to the sittings of the tariff board or to the sittings of the trade and industry commission.

I suppose we
will have to let the matter pass with that somewhat lame excuse. I do not think the absence of any one should be accepted by the committee as the reason for the government not being able to give an explanation.

The minister is creating a precedent. In the past any gratuity or emolument paid to anyone receiving a regular salary was shown with the name of the person receiving the payment. This $15,000 is to be paid out by the treasury board to officials already in receipt of regular salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Without discussing the
merits of this practice, I would say to the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) that I can give him a number of instances under the regime of my right hon. friend where a similar procedure was followed. Were there any anonymous workers?
The Secretary of State put in considerable overtime on this matter; will he not get anything extra?

I have done a great deal of extra work during the past five years, but I am not asking for any gratuities. I am not criticizing the vote; I am criticizing the manner in which it is being expended.

I have never seen them.

required, $22,735.

My hon. friend is rather satirical. The work of this bureau has increased enormously. I cannot remember a session of parliament when there was so much work in the way of translations. It must be remembered that the evidence and report of the price spreads commission involved a large amount of work. For instance, the translation required 5,400 printed pages, while the type for both editions of the report weighed 46 tons. I thought it unfair to impose all this extra translation work upon men who were working under a strain at times, and I asked the civil1 service commission to make a recommendation to the treasury board1 for temporary assistance. I can give my hon. friend all the details of this item if he desires.

I am not concerned with the details. In connection with the previous vote the minister stated that it was to cover remuneration for extra work, and I should like to know if any portion of this vote will go to the translators for fhe extra work they have done.

This vote is to provide the additional translation services which were necessary to take care of the extra work. In this connection I should like to refer to a question asked on June 12 by the hon. member for L'lslet (Mr. Fafard). This question reads:
Does the government intend to have a French translation made of bulletin No. 72: "Birds of Canada," by P. A. Taverner, also memoranda numbers 126: "Botanical Exploration of the North Shore of the St. Lawrence," by H. St. John; 146: "Retreat of the Last Ice-Sheet in Eastern Canada," by Ernest Antevs; 154: "Geology of Anticosti Island," by Twenhofel; 162: "Peat Bogs in Southeastern Canada," by Vaino Auer?
I replied that the translation of such departmental bulletins was within the discretion of the department issuing the bulletin and that up to date we had received no requests for the translation of the documents referred to. Before making my answer I inquired of the bureau for translations and I was told that they had received no requests for the translation of these documents. I had thought that possibly under the stress of translation, work these might have been overlooked. After making that reply, on June 14 one of the journals passed a very severe stricture upon the Secretary of State for making a reply such as he did, but I believe its article was due to a complete misunderstanding of the facts. For instance, bulletin or memoir No. 126 by Harold St. John, on Botanical Explorations of the North Shore of the St. Lawrence, was, I find on inquiry, published by the director of the Department of the Victoria Memorial Museum on March 25, 1922, and it has been distributed since that date. No translation of this memoir into French has been published. I do not conceive it to b.e my duty at the present time to go back for fourteen years in order to look over all the bulletins to find out whether or not they have been translated into French. Bulletin or memoir No. 146, by Ernest Antevs, on the Retreat of the Last Ice-Sheet in Eastern Canada, was published in 1925 by the director of the geological survey of the Department of Mines, and no translation was made into French. Of course I have not been going back into all these memoirs, of which there are hundreds, to find out whether, antecedent to the formation of the bureau of translation, they were translated. The same may be said of bulletin or memoir No. 154, on the Geology of Anticosti Island by W. H. Twenhofel, which was published by the director of the geological survey of the Department of Mines in 1928. No translation of this into French has yet been made, and there has been no 
demand for one. Bulletin or memoir No. 162 by Vaino Auer, on Peat Bogs in Southeastern 'Canada, was published in English alone as a bulletin prior to the formation of this government.
There is one point however to which attention might be given. There has recently been published by the acting director of the National Museum of Canada bulletin No. 72 on Birds of Canada by P. A. Taverner which has just been 'issued to the public and is now available in English at the price of $2 per volume if requests are made either to the Department of Mines or to the Department of Public Printing and Stationery. No request has yet reached the Department of the Secretary of State with regard to the translation of that bulletin into French. I can well understand a suggestion being made in the French journals that it should be translated into French, but upon inquiry I find that the decision whether that bulletin will be translated and published in French will depend to a considerable extent upon the probable demand for a French edition. So far there has been, no special demand, due probably to the fact that in 1922 there was published by the .director of the geological survey a splendid edition in French, which is still available, of Mr. Taverner's memoire No. 10-1, Les Oisseaux de l'est du Canada, which reached a second edition in that year, and which largely forms the basis of the English edition which was published this year. Moreover in connection with this recent English edition now available there has been provided an index in the French language as well as in English with the idea that those who wish to make cross references to the two volumes might readily do so. But if there is any considerable demand for a French edition of this later work, which includes not only the birds of eastern Canada but some birds of western Canada as well, I have no doubt, the Minister of Mines will ask for an appropriation for its publication. The minister has been absent for a few days, and since this question arose I have not had an opportunity of speaking to him. I did speak to him when it came out in English just a few weeks ago, and he told me that he thought an edition of it in French might be required. But upon investigation the fact appears that those two French editions of the same author's wTork on the birds of eastern Canada have largely gone to the province of Quebec for study there. If there is any considerable demand for a French edition of Mr. Taverner's recent work, though it is a very expensive one, I have no doubt the wishes of my French Canadian col-

Supply-Miscellaneous-Electoral Officer
leagues would receive favourable consideration. I thought I would like to make that statement for fear there might be some misunderstanding in regard to the matter.

I do not intend! to
continue the discussion on that point because I do not think this is the proper time for it, but may I say that in the Department of Mines there are many most interesting publications in English. A large proportion of the population of Canada feels, and I think quite properly so, if a work is important enough to be published in English, it ought to be sufficiently important to be published in French. I am not unmindful however of the fact that French translations of many of those publications are not asked) for, but that portion of the population nevertheless takes the attitude-and I think it is a proper one-that if financial conditions permit, one should not even have to ask for or to insist upon a French edition, but that both editions should be published concurrently. If a publication in English is important enough to be distributed throughout foreign countries in universities and museums, it should be important enough to be distributed in French. Probably when the proper time comes to discuss that question, I shall speak at greater length. I just wanted to make these remarks at the moment.

My hon. friend will, I am
sure, agree with me that this is not my duty as the minister having charge of the bureau for translations. The bureau for translations is prepared to d'o its work, but it is for the national museum1, the Geological survey or others to ask for the necessary appropriations for publications and to request officially that a translation be made.

May I tell the Secretary
of State that a great mistake made last year was in not paying attention to my colleague, the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier), who had a wonderful plan to submit to my hon. friend with regard to translations. Had the minister been more conciliatory at that time, he would have received excellent suggestions from the senior member for Ottawa.

I thought the Secretary of
State was one of the most conciliatory members of the house.

In connection with this item of 822,735 to provide for salaries and- expenses of the bureau for translations, further amount required, the the Secretary of State mentioned that this
was due partly to the price spreadb investigation. It would be interesting to some of us to know just the total cost to the country of that investigation. It is cropping up here and there, and we have no idea1 what the total cost has been. I wonder whether the Secretary of State or some other member of the government would undertake to give us the full details.

I cannot give those details.
They are not in the Department of the Secretary of State; they would have to be gathered from several departments, and I am afraid the time is a little late for that.

It is of
importance that the people of the country should know just what the price spreads investigation has cost, particularly because it has been such a washout Bo far as legislation is concerned.

Not only that, but we
must know where to pub the report. It is so tremendous that one needs a special room to put it in and it serves no purpose, it is no good.

Item agreed to.
Chief electoral officer-salaries and contingencies of office-further amount required, $40,000.

This is a new item. At
previous general elections such expenses as the salaries of temporary employees, printing, stationery, et cetera in connection with approaching general elections were charged to elections and paid out of the consolidated revenue fund. But the comptroller of the treasury has recently ruled that they are not properly chargeable to election expenses as such and must be paid out of some special appropriation provided in the estimates. We have no appropriation in the estimates except the ordinary contingency fund of the chief electoral officer. Therefore in order to comply with the requirements of the treasury department I have asked that this sum of 840,000 be provided for this purpose.

When do
these general election expenses begin?

So far as I am concerned
the sooner they begin the better.

There is a matter I should
like to bring to the attention of the minister, which ought to be remedied under this vote, even if we have to increase the amount. Last fall the list was made up of people

entitled to vote. Each member of parliament and certain other people were given, I think, three copies, either typewritten or handwritten, of the list as made up at that date.
I did not know that.

Well, they were. It was,
of course, of great value. One of the first essentials of an election is to get on the list, and the second is to know whether you are on or not. Some months later, after the lists had been printed, we each got twenty-one copies of the list of each polling division. Up to that date we knew exactly where we were. When a man came to me and asked if he were on the list I could tell him. Now we have had a revision, which is just completed, and according to the advice I get from the department I have no means of knowing whether I am on the list or not, whether I am qualified to be a candidate or not, because to be a candidate one must be on some list. The procedure to be adopted apparently is that we are to be furnished with no list when the revision is completed but after the revised list is printed we will get the twenty-one copies as before. Those lists may be furnished to us perhaps a week before the election.
Oh, no.

It may well be; and in
scattered country districts it will be impossible to get those lists out to the polling stations in time. As I said, one of the first essentials is to know who is on the list and who is not. A man is entitled to know whether he is on or not. Under the plan that apparently has been adopted, or the regulations, it is not possible, unless by the courtesy of the registrar who may tell me, perhaps illegally, that I am on, for me to know whether I am on or anyone else is. I suggest the procedure should be followed that was followed last fall, that every member of parliament and others who are entitled to get it should be furnished with, say, two copies, typewritten or handwritten-it would suffice if they were only of the corrections. We want to know the people who have been added and those who have been struck off, and we want to know it soon after the revision is complete. It will be grossly unfair to a great many people if they have to guess whether they are on the list. We should get two copies, one for our own use and one to send to our representative in each polling station. I think the house will see the need for that, especially in the country. The cost would not be great, especially if it were limited to the corrections; let us take the expense of correcting our lists ourselves.

The typewritten lists which were given out, to which the hon. member refers, were not given out by the dominion franchise commissioner. Each registrar was instructed to give information to each candidate with regard to the preparation of the lists. I have no doubt that the registrar in the district which my hon. friend represents prepared for him these copies-
He was compelled to do it by law.
I know no such law. I think it was done simply as a matter of courtesy.
No, pardon me; it was done by law-it is part of the act.
Then the same law will probably apply-

No; I am advised by the head of the department that that is not to be tb.e rule, and that is what I am kicking about. I shall be perfectly satisfied if the same system is to be carried out as was carried out before, not by courtesy of any individual but by law, but I have been advised by the head of the department that the law is that we are not to be given any lists until they are printed, and they may not be available until perhaps within a week of the election.

If my hon, friend will see that the electoral lists from his district are sent in in proper time, they should arrive by the tenth of July, and if so they will certainly foe printed by the fifteenth or twentieth.
Of July?

Yes, certainly, July. We have on the lists of last year-they say I carry these figures about with me for the convenience of the leader of the opposition-
5.800.000	names. Those names are all in type. We have on hand 350 tons of type for these names. The suggestion has been made by some newspaper correspondents that there are 250,000 new voters coming on the lists. I doubt that very much, but suppose there are
250.000	coming on and 250,000 removals and changes. I am told that the changes in the country districts are limited chiefly to those who have passed from this earthly sphere, and they are not numerous.
And some are coming of age.

We have a well organized printing establishment; I think it is the best organized and most efficient anywhere in Canada. When we were printing these names, working sometimes the whole twenty-four hours in order to comply with the wishes of

Supply-Miscellaneous-Electoral Officer
the right hon. leader of the opposition and enable me to fulfil my promises to him, we printed 100,000 a day. So far as printing the new lists, is concerned, if we get the names in, setting the new lines on the linotype for
500,000	names will be done in ten days. This talk in the newspapers about the election being long delayed because of delay in the printing bureau is due to the imaginative qualities of some newspaper correspondents.

If that statement is correct- of course I do not doubt the hon. gentleman's veracity-and he is able to deliver the goods, my complaint falls to the. ground. I do not like to say it when he is absent, but I think the Prime Minister himself said it would be late in September before these lists could be printed.

There is no possibility now at this late stage of changing the law to which the hon. member refers. But the dominion franchise officer is an officer of this house and reports to the house and the government through the Secretary of State. I shall therefore take the earliest opportunity of consulting him, and suggesting that instructions be given that every facility be granted to candidates or prospective candidates to obtain the former printed lists, with such corrections as have been made, for use in their preliminary work in connection with the election.

The hon. member for Comox-Albemi has raised what in my opinion is a very important question. From the remarks of the Secretary of State I take it that the same procedure will be followed that was adopted by the registrars in our various ridings when the enumerators completed their lists, in other words that we wTill receive not a printed but a typewrtten list of the names added in the revision that has been going on since April 1. That is, the list will show the names struck off during the month of April, the names added during May and June, the names transferred and matters of that kind. Will all members and defeated candidates receive typewritten copies immediately the revising officers report to the dominion franchise commissioner at Ottawa? Will the same procedure be followed that was followed during the preparation of the lists in 1934; is that what I understand?

What I have said is this: The dominion franchise officer is an officer of this house, and those registrars who are appointed by him are also officers of this house. I will convey to the dominion franchise commissioner the view that has been expressed as being the general view of the house, and I have no doubt that the suggestion will be carried into effect.

Let me tell the hon. member for West Lambton that I can answer his question better than the minister can answer it, apparently. I have in my possession a letter from the head of the department, dated within the last two days, stating exactly what I have said, that we will not get the lists for which my hon. friend has asked but that we will have to wait until they are all printed. The minister says that can be done by July 20. If that can be done it will be entirely satisfactory, but I beg leave to express doubt as to that. I certainly have that letter, in which I am told that the revised lists will not be furnished, as they were last fall, but that we will have to wait until they are all printed, which in some constituencies may mean a delay of months.

That is exactly what I understood, and I object very strongly. When that list is eventually printed the names that have been added will simply appear in alphabetical or geographical order, and unless one has an organization as efficient as the Secretary of State has in the riding of St. Lawrence-St. George one will not be able to tell exactly what names have been added. I strenuously object; if I have to hunt out the names that have been added I cannot possibly see them all in a week or ten days and convert them to the proper way of thinking. I want to know what names have been added to the list in this revision, and I think every member, every defeated candidate and every nominated candidate is entitled to that information. As I understand it, that is all the hon. member for Comox-Alberni desires, and I think that is all any hon. member desires. I think in fairness we are entitled to know what names have been added, what names have been transferred and what names have been struek off the list since the establishment of the basic list in 1934. As I understand it the Secretary of State simply says that we will be given a list, and if we have efficient organizations we will be able to check off those who were on the list in 1934, so we will know what names have been added since that time. Surely the hon. gentleman sees the point we are urging. Surely it would be a very simple matter to have extra copies made when reporting to the franchise commissioner. It is not too late; the revision does not close until to-morrow, so it should

be a simple matter to strike an extra copy or two. If the Secretary of State will say that he will so instruct the franchise commissioner-
He is not under my instructions.

I am sorry, because I feel sure the Secretary of State would do so. In view of the fact that the hon. gentleman has expressed the feeling that the franchise commissioner would follow a suggestion made by the house I again urge that when the revising officers report to the franchise commissioner they send a copy to the candidate, and I think that will meet the situation.
May I ask the Secretary of State if it would1 not be possible for some member of the ministry to bring this request to the attention of the franchise commissioner?
I offered to do so.
Then if my hon. friend will1 do that I think he will meet the situation.

There is more to it than that. Some names have been struck off and others added to the basic list that has been supplied to us. As I understand the law, and I am speaking from memory, as a retiring member of this house my horn, friend is entitled to receive twenty-one copies of the new print, and certainly he will receive them. Through those names struck off a line will be drawn; for those names added new lines will be inserted. When the commissioner approves that list one copy will be sent to the printing bureau for the revision of the list in the composition room, and that will be carried
(Mr. Gray.]
out. I think it would meet the desire of my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni if the registrar were instructed1 to give each member who desired it a copy of the revised list which he sends in to the dominion franchise commissioner.
Two copies.

Well), I will; suggest to the dominion franchise commissioner that this appears to be the view of the house. That is as far as I can go. It would be a very delicate matter for me to interfere, but I will convey to him the view of the house.
I am sure if the Secretary of State does that the franchise officer will be only too ready to meet the wishes of the hon. members of the house.

Before the item is carried, may I ask the minister the cost of preparing the lists for the last general election, and what will be the cost in the present year, including the cost of printing and purchasing those tons of lead for galleys?

I cannot answer that. Those matters do not come under my department, and I have no charge of such expenditures in any way, shape or form. I have charge of the printing, in connection with which I have made full returns to the house which are available to the hon. member. As to the printing of the lists for the last election, the house is fully informed. I cannot give any other information because it does not come under my department.

The minister states that the house is fully informed. He tells us nothing; how can we know? The lists were prepared in a certain way to effect economies, and now the minister cannot tell us what economies have been made. I remember distinctly that when the minister rose to submit certain legislation he said, "Here, we will save money this way." I ask him now, how did you save money that way; if the records are in the house>
look after them.

The hon. member is evidently suffering from an hallucination induced by the exuberance of his own imagination. I made no such statement to the house. In the statement I made I dealt only with the cost of composition and printing.

I am not a somnambulist, and I am not dreaming; I remember what was said, and you must remember it yourself. We heard about saving money; I heard it, I think

every hon. member heard it, and it is printed in Hansard. That is the reason the lists were made in a certain way. The legislation providing for the manner of preparing the lists was absurd. It has taken too much material; it has taken a long time, and not only that, the names are wrongly printed. The collection of the galleys has been badly done. Further, there will be a waste of paper because of revision of lists and because the government has waited too long to bring on the election. When I support the rights of the people and the policy of economy the minister states that I am suffering from hallucinations. Is he not ashamed of himself when he speaks that way? speechtext: Perhaps I may be allowed to say a word; I happen to have some knowledge of the item, having been at pains to make particular inquiry regarding it.
